title: Sign Off the Promises, Not the Paragraphs: A Claim-Strength Linter for Model-Drafted Docs
summary:
A model can draft your walkthrough, your config table, and most of your troubleshooting prose, but it must never be the last author of a sentence that promises behavior. That single rule is the whole workflow below: the model owns procedure, a human owns promises, and a small linter decides which sentences count as promises. Everything else here is machinery for enforcing that split on every pull request.

The artifact is two files and about eighty lines of Python. One file inventories promise-bearing sentences and scores their strength; the other records a human sign-off with a live evidence pointer for each one. Existing doc tooling usually validates links, spelling, or style, so it happily ships a sentence that claims an operation is atomic when nothing tests atomicity.

title: Skip Is Not a Freeze: Revocable Seeded Freezes for Agent Patches
summary:
A skipped test is not a frozen test. It is a deleted test that still compiles. The difference matters the moment an agent starts shipping patches into the same suite, because a skip has no expiry, no signature, and no obligation to ever come back.

This post describes a freeze that revokes itself: every frozen test carries the seed that reproduces its failure, and every agent patch must re-run that seed and classify the result. If the seeded run now fails deterministically, the freeze is void — that is a regression, not flake.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
summary:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
summary:
This is fascinating:

The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening.

It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another...

title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
summary:
It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it.

Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result.

I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that.

title: MCP tool authorization: a gateway deny counts only when the server shows no side effect
summary:
Putting a gateway in front of an MCP server gives you a policy enforcement point on one network path. It does not prove the upstream server cannot be reached another way. A test that stops at the gateway's decision log checks the gateway's claim against the gateway's own records: the request was denied, the log says so, test passed.

The question that matters is different: can a call the policy denies still cause a side effect on the upstream server? You answer that at the server and in the state it changes. This article proposes a test matrix built around that one assertion, with a harmless fixture server that keeps two records: one of every call its handlers receive, and one of the state it actually changed. The matrix covers discovery, invocation, a policy change between the two, an unapproved sensitive action, a direct call that skips the gateway, and a telemetry-only path that no gateway decides on.

title: An AI poller cost us almost 27 USD in one day: the 40-line spend guard we added
summary:
One day in July our AI bill reached almost 27 USD in a single day. Nobody had asked for it. This post is the short version of what went wrong and the small guard we run so it does not happen silently again. The code is about 40 lines of Python with no extra packages.

What happened

We had an agent task that woke up every 3 minutes to check an inbox. Each wake-up was a full model call. The scheduler had registered that task 4 times, so it really ran about 80 times an hour.

That alone would have been cheap, because the task used a free model. Then the free model started answering with rate limit errors (HTTP 429). Our model router had a fallback list, and the next entry was a paid model. Every 429 quietly became a paid call. Nothing watched the spend, so we only saw it hours later.
